title: NVIDIA Vera CPU at Hot Chips 2026
gist: NVIDIA detailed Vera, its 88-core in-house Arm server CPU built on the new Olympus core, deliberately optimizing IPC and single-thread latency over core count because agentic workflows are latency-bound rather than throughput-bound. Vera splits into six dies on one interposer with eight 128-bit LPDDR5X controllers, 96 lanes of PCIe/CXL, NVLink-C2C to Rubin GPUs, and rack-wide confidential computing.

insights.claim: Server economics have favored renting out cores and thus designs with very large numbers of weaker cores, but that model does not work for AI workflows where higher single-threaded performance is needed.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Cuts against the core-count race Intel and AMD are running, and implies core-count-per-dollar is the wrong metric for AI-adjacent CPU demand.
insights.quote: Meanwhile server economics have favored renting out cores, and thus chip designs for a very large number of cores, but weaker CPU cores overall. But this does not work for AI workflows, where higher single-threaded performance is needed.
insights.locator: Shifting gears over to the Vera CPU

insights.claim: Vera focuses heavily on IPC over core count, landing at 88 CPU cores flanked by eight 128-bit LPDDR5X memory controllers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: 88 cores against 136-256 core rivals means NVIDIA is competing on a different axis and will not be comparable on standard core-count benchmarks.
insights.quote: The large chip focuses heavily on IPC over core count, leaving it with 88 CPU cores altogether, and flanked by eight 128-bit LPDDR5X memory controllers.
insights.locator: At a high level, Vera is designed to be a very modern

insights.claim: Latency drove the design philosophy because agents move from task to task and the sooner one task completes the sooner the next begins, which benefits high-IPC architectures.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes CPU value in AI systems around task-completion latency, a metric that favors NVIDIA's design and disfavors throughput-optimized rivals.
insights.quote: Agents move from task to task; the sooner they can complete one task, the sooner they can move on to the next.
insights.locator: A big part of that design philosophy was also on latency

insights.claim: The Olympus core carries a huge 10-wide decode front-end with massive buffers and an even bigger backend to consume the decoded instructions.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A 10-wide decode places Olympus among the widest server cores disclosed, indicating NVIDIA is spending serious area per core rather than replicating IP.
insights.locator: Here is a quick look at the Olympus CPU core logical diagram

insights.claim: NVIDIA implemented statically partitioned spatial multithreading rather than conventional resource-sharing SMT, claiming the same performance level while being less susceptible to noise from threads fighting over CPU resources.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Determinism-oriented multithreading targets the tail-latency problem that hurts agentic serving, a design choice worth watching if it spreads.
insights.quote: Though they went with statically partitioned spatial multithreading, rather than resource sharing across multiple threads in a CPU.
insights.locator: Olympus is agentic-first, but not agentic-only

insights.claim: NVIDIA's SPEC CPU 2026 subset shows agentic workloads close to 1.8x and data processing workloads closer to 1.5x, though NVIDIA reiterates these are proxy workloads.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The vendor-selected benchmark subset and proxy caveat mean the 1.8x figure should be discounted until independent agentic benchmarks exist.
insights.locator: For their big benchmark reveal last month

insights.claim: Vera needed more silicon than a single reticle-limited die allows, so NVIDIA split it into 6 dies on a single interposer, keeping a monolithic die for the compute cores while moving memory and I/O to their own chiplets.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A monolithic compute die plus disaggregated IO is a different chiplet philosophy from AMD and Intel, with different yield and packaging supply implications.
insights.quote: The end result was that they split it up into 6 dies, retaining a monolithic die for the compute cores, but moving the memory and I/O to their own chiplets.
insights.locator: To build Vera, NVIDIA needed more silicon

insights.claim: The Vera system I/O die carries 96 lanes of PCIe and CXL, which NVIDIA uses to connect to ConnectX NICs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Ties Vera's I/O budget directly to NVIDIA's own networking attach, reinforcing full-stack lock-in per socket.
insights.locator: Vera is designed to work with the most valuable chips

insights.claim: The NVLink-C2C interface pairs Vera with NVIDIA's Rubin GPUs but can also connect to anything else implementing NVLink-C2C, or to another Vera chip for a 2P pure CPU setup.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Opening NVLink-C2C to third-party silicon extends NVIDIA's fabric as an industry standard while keeping Vera at the center.
insights.locator: At a high level, Vera is designed to be a very modern

insights.claim: LPDDR5X was chosen for Vera's memory subsystem because it was the most energy efficient option and energy efficiency is a key constraint on modern systems.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Another data center CPU committing to LPDDR over DDR5, expanding a memory-type shift that changes DRAM vendor mix.
insights.quote: It was the most energy efficient choice, and energy efficiency is a key constraint to modern systems.
insights.locator: LPDDR5X was the obvious choice for a memory subsystem

themes.theme: The performance frontier and Groq LPX3

insights.claim: NVIDIA's performance frontier frames the trade-off between token throughput and user interactivity: high batching maximizes token generation but makes response time poor, and Vera Rubin is meant to push the frontier out in both directions.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The frontier curve is the reusable frame for comparing all inference hardware claims, since any single throughput number depends on where on the curve it was measured.
insights.quote: their performance frontier, the trade-off between token throughput and user interactivity
insights.locator: NVIDIA has shown off this curve

insights.claim: At higher interactivity levels, Vera Rubin offers up to 30 times the total throughput of Grace Blackwell, but the gain is heavily dependent on where you sit on the curve because Grace Blackwell collapsed at an earlier point.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The headline 30x is a curve-position artifact, not a general speedup; the real claim is a later collapse point under interactivity pressure.
insights.quote: Though it is heavily dependent on where you are on the curve; Grace Blackwell collapsed at an earlier point that Vera Rubin.
insights.locator: And here is another look at how throughput compares

insights.claim: NVIDIA now offers Groq LPX3 racks using Groq's dedicated decode-acceleration hardware for customers needing higher interactivity than Vera Rubin CPUs and GPUs alone can sustain, with long-context decode claimed four times faster than current public services.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: NVIDIA productizing a third-party decode accelerator signals its own GPUs have a real interactivity ceiling and creates a new category of decode-specialist silicon.
insights.quote: NVIDIA now has its Grorq LPX3 racks, which use Groq’s dedicated hardware for decode acceleration to push out the curve farther to allow for very high interactivity rates without performance collapsing.
insights.locator: And for customers who need more than what Vera Rubin can do

insights.claim: AI is presented as a full workflow touching multiple tools and types of computation rather than one task or query, so a system optimized for a single use case cannot win.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Justifies platform bundling over best-of-breed component competition, the strategic core of NVIDIA's full-stack pitch.
insights.quote: And it is not one task or query, but it is a full workflow that touches multiple tools and types of computation. You cannot just optimize for one use case and win.
insights.locator: NVIDIA is starting things off by framing this talk

insights.claim: Vera and Rubin were designed for full-stack confidential compute across the entire rack, requiring intense co-design between CPU, GPU, and NIC, with the GPU checking requests from the CPU using per-core encryption keys.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Rack-wide confidential compute is hard for mix-and-match vendors to replicate, deepening the co-design moat around NVIDIA racks.

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims tamper-proof operation only when used with a suitable software platform such as its own DOCA, attaching a software condition to the security guarantee.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The security claim is conditional on NVIDIA software, converting a hardware feature into a software attach driver.
insights.quote: This ensures the system is tamper-proof – at least when used with a suitable software platform, such as NVIDIA’s DOCA software platform.

insights.claim: Vera is NVIDIA's most ambitious effort yet to expand its presence in the server CPU market, with the company looking to capture a larger piece of the pie with a specialized-but-powerful CPU.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Frames Vera as a share-taking move against x86 server CPU incumbents, not merely a host processor for GPUs.
insights.quote: It is also their most ambitious effort yet to expand their overall presence in the server CPU market, as NVIDIA is looking to capture a larger piece of the pie with their specialized-but-powerful CPU.
insights.locator: For the third and final presentation

insights.claim: Vera will be sold both inside NVL72 rackscale systems and as individual Vera servers through NVIDIA and its partners.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Standalone Vera servers put NVIDIA in direct competition with EPYC and Xeon sockets, widening the front where x86 must defend.
insights.locator: In closing, Vera is available as part of NVL72
